tip: 'Il est essentiel que' takes the subjunctive: 'fasse', not 'fait'. Judgments of necessity trigger this mood.
'Dont' bundles in the 'of whom/whose': 'l'auteur dont j'ai lu tous les livres' = the author of whom I've read all the books.
'Allons-y' literally means 'let's go there' – that little 'y' stands in for a place English just leaves out.
'Regarder' already means 'look at' – there's no word for 'at'. You look the view directly: 'regardez cette vue'.
Doubt undercuts certainty, so French flips to the subjunctive: 'je doute qu'il vienne', not 'vient' – the same switch you get after 'ne pas penser que'.
In a positive command the pronoun follows ('lève-toi'), but negate it and 'te' jumps back in front: 'ne te lève pas'.
In a positive command the pronoun follows the verb, joined by a hyphen: 'appelle-moi'.
'Dans dix minutes' = in ten minutes from now. Use 'dans', not 'en' – 'en dix minutes' would mean it takes ten minutes.
In 'Dépêche-toi, on va être en retard', 'on' means 'we' – but the verb keeps its he/she form: 'on va', not 'on allons'.
'Devrais' is the conditional of 'devoir' and means 'should', not 'must' – it's softer advice: 'tu devrais appeler'.
'Il est possible que' expresses uncertainty and triggers the subjunctive: 'que nous déménagions'.
'Plaire' flips the subject and object: 'te plaît' turns 'what you like' into 'what pleases you' – you're the receiver: 'ce qui te plaît'.
French says 'les mains', not 'your hands' – with body parts you usually use the reflexive plus 'the': 'lave-toi les mains'.
To rewind and imagine a different past, pair 'si' + the had-form with a would-have clause: 'si j'avais su, je ne serais pas venu' = had I known, I wouldn't have come.
'Boirais' is 'would drink', but add 'bien' and it means 'I could really go for one': 'je boirais bien un thé'.
In an if-then sentence 'si' skips the conditional and takes the imperfect ('commençait'); the 'would' half gets it: 'on finirait'.
'Le samedi' doesn't mean one Saturday – with the article it means 'on Saturdays', every week: 'ouvert le samedi'.
You say 'parler de quelque chose', so 'the book everyone talks about' needs 'dont', the word that swallows that 'de'.
'Avait quitté' = 'had left'. For the earlier of two past events French uses this past-of-the-past, before plain 'a sonné'.
'Bien que' (although) takes the subjunctive: 'bien qu'il pleuve'.
You play 'du piano', not 'le piano' – instruments take 'jouer de', while sports take 'jouer à': 'jouer au foot'.
Adjectives of emotion + 'que' trigger the subjunctive: 'soit', not 'est'.
'Devoir' in the conditional turns 'must' into gentle advice: 'tu devrais lire' = you should read, softer than 'tu dois' = you have to.
'Il est dommage que' expresses regret and takes the subjunctive: 'puissions', from 'pouvoir'.
A superlative claim tips the que-clause into the subjunctive: 'la plus belle ville que j'aie jamais visitée' uses 'aie', not 'ai'.
'Pourvu que' (provided that) triggers the subjunctive: 'tu fasses attention'.
In formal French a 'ne' with no negative meaning can appear after 'avant que': 'avant que tu ne t'en ailles'.
'Elle exige que' (she demands that) triggers the subjunctive: 'soient', not 'sont'.
There's no word for 'let's' in French – the '-ons' ending carries it. 'Partageons' = 'let's share'. Any nous-form verb can become a suggestion this way.
In a positive command the pronoun hops behind the verb, joined by a hyphen: 'explique-lui' – but negate it and the pronoun jumps back in front: 'ne lui explique pas'.
